title: More threat data is useful only if security teams can act on it

blocks.text: Security teams have access to more threat intelligence than ever, but the volume of information can create another problem: figuring out what actually needs attention.

Security Operations Centers are already handling large numbers of alerts every day, often with fewer people than they need. Attackers are also moving quickly, leaving analysts less time to determine which indicators point to an active threat and which can be deprioritized.

This puts a practical limit on the value of threat intelligence. An organization may have extensive information about malicious activity, but analysts still need to sort through that information before they can act on it.

Kaspersky is adding new AI capabilities to its Threat Intelligence Portal to address that problem. The features include AI-generated summaries of human-readable threat intelligence and support for the Model Context Protocol, or MCP, which allows third-party AI applications to connect to the portal.
Making threat intelligence easier to review
During an investigation or threat-hunting exercise, analysts can encounter hundreds of Indicators of Compromise (IoCs), along with reports covering threat actors, campaigns, and related activity.

Kaspersky’s new summarization feature condenses information associated with an indicator into a shorter overview. The aim is to give analysts enough context to decide whether an IoC warrants a closer look without requiring them to immediately work through every available source.
The company says the summaries are generated from selected source datasets, allowing analysts to see the context behind the information rather than receiving an isolated AI-generated answer.

The feature can also be used with IoCs discovered through open-source intelligence searches. Analysts can use the AI-generated summaries to get an initial view of the information associated with an entity and determine where a deeper investigation is needed.

This does not replace the analyst’s role in evaluating the intelligence. It changes the first stage of the process. Analysts can use the summary to narrow their focus, then examine the underlying information when an indicator or threat actor requires further investigation.

That can be particularly useful for teams dealing with large volumes of intelligence, as well as less-experienced analysts who may otherwise have to work through extensive information before establishing where to begin.
Connecting threat intelligence to AI applications
Kaspersky is also introducing MCP connectivity, allowing organizations to connect their own AI applications or third-party AI tools to the Threat Intelligence Portal.

MCP provides a way for AI applications to interact with external tools and data sources. For threat intelligence, that means an AI application can query information from Kaspersky’s portal when it needs it, rather than requiring analysts to manually move information between separate systems.
Instead of limiting AI to tasks such as summarizing reports, organizations can connect it to external sources that allow it to retrieve information as part of a larger workflow.

Kaspersky says its threat intelligence is built on more than 25 petabytes of proprietary threat context. That amount of data can provide security teams with a broad view of malicious activity, but it also illustrates the problem that AI is being used to address. The more intelligence available to analysts, the more difficult it can become to review everything manually.

For security teams dealing with high alert volumes and staffing constraints, the value of AI may therefore be less about producing more intelligence and more about making existing intelligence easier to work with.
Kaspersky’s new features are aimed at reducing the time between finding a piece of threat intelligence and determining what it means for an organization’s security operation.
